title: Four Young Men in Babylon
sum: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem, takes King Jehoiakim and some of the temple vessels, and orders his chief eunuch to bring in young Israelites from the royal family and the nobles to be trained for the king's service. Four of them, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, are given Babylonian names and a daily ration from the king's table.

Daniel decides not to defile himself with the royal food and wine. God gives him favor with the official in charge, and a ten-day test of plant food and water shows the four looking better than those who eat the king's rich food. God gives them learning, and Daniel the gift of understanding visions and dreams. When the king interviews them he finds no one like them, ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters. Daniel stays until the first year of Cyrus.
readings: As a report of what happened

Daniel and his friends were taken in 605 BC, trained in the Babylonian scribal schools, and stayed faithful to the law in a foreign court. Details such as the new names, the three-year course and the Persian word for food belong to a writer who knew the court; the difference between 'third' and 'fourth' year is a matter of counting.
As a tale for later Jews

The chapter is a model story for Jews living under foreign rule, written to show that a person can serve the king and keep the covenant. On this reading the date may be later (third to second century BC), the Persian words show a late writer, and the gaps (the king not knowing Daniel in 2:25) show separate stories.

Whatever its date, the chapter belongs to a type: a Jew at a foreign court, tested, refused, vindicated (Joseph, Esther, Daniel). It sets the book's two themes, God as the one who gives and loyalty at a cost.

views.H: On the traditional dating the chapter is an eyewitness opening in 605 BC, from the first deportation to the first year of Cyrus (539/538 BC). On the Maccabean dating it is a tale told as if from Babylon for readers in 167-164 BC, and Nebuchadnezzar a stand-in for Antiochus IV. Both sides agree on the verses: the siege, the vessels, the food test.
views.C: Critics point to the Persian loanword for 'rich food', the use of 'Chaldean' for a learned class and the doubtful 'third year' as signs of a later writer, and to the break in the story at 2:25. Defenders answer each in turn (see the notes at 1:1, 1:4, 1:5).
views.J: The rabbis counted Daniel among the Writings. The Talmud argues over whether he and his friends were made eunuchs (Sanhedrin 93b).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Daniel a model of faithful witness in a foreign land (Hebrews 11 alludes to this book) and in the test of the four a picture of holiness without withdrawal.
views.F: Chapter 1 has little to say about the end, but it opens the story of Gentile world rule that Daniel 2 and 7 follow, and that futurist, historicist and Maccabean readers each carry to a different end.

deep.h: Which witnesses were read for this edition
deep.b: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, the Hebrew and Aramaic text of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), read word by word. The Qumran copies of these chapters were read through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription: 1QDan-a (1Q71) for 1:10-17, 2:2-6 and the Aramaic of chapter 2, 4QDan-a (4Q112) for 1:16-20 and 2:9-49, and for chapter 3 1QDan-b (1Q72) and 4QDan-d (4Q115) as well as 4QDan-a. Restored words in a transcription are never counted as a scroll's reading. The Greek was read in two forms: the Old Greek as Swete prints it from Codex Chisianus, and Theodotion. Swete's Old Greek is a single manuscript, so differences are named by witness; the critical text is Ziegler's Göttingen edition. Where a note cites a reading from that edition or from another Old Greek witness, it says who reports it.

The test is carefully told: Daniel asks the official to risk nothing but ten days, the official agrees, and the result is then credited to God (1:15, 17). The passage never says plant food is better than meat (see the note at 1:15). It does not say why the king's food defiled either; the main answers are given in the note at 1:8. What the story does say is that the king's table is a place of obligation, and that Daniel keeps his own limit with courtesy and a reasoned request. The same attitude marks him in the lions' den (Daniel 6) and in his fast of mourning (Daniel 10:2-3).

deep.title: Claude's theory: Daniel opens in Shinar, the land of Babel
deep.b: Daniel 1:2 is the only place in the Bible that says the temple vessels were taken to Shinar, the name of the plain of the tower (Genesis 11:2); the other accounts say Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:7; Jeremiah 27:16-22). Daniel 3:1 puts the great statue on a plain (Hebrew biq'ah in Genesis 11:2, Aramaic biq'a in Daniel 3:1) in the province of Babylon, summoning every "people, nation and language" to one act at one signal. My suggestion is that the author writes the first half of the book as a second Babel: the world's peoples gathered by a king to a human-made monument, and God answering by bringing the proud low (chapters 3 to 5). Babel echoes in Daniel are noticed by some commentators (for example in Daniel 4:30, 'Is this not the great Babylon I have built?'), and Zechariah 5:11 also puts a house for Wickedness in Shinar. The pairing of 'Shinar' and 'plain' across chapters 1 and 3 may overlap with published work. It rests on shared vocabulary only.
deep.refs: Genesis 11:1-9; Daniel 1:2; Daniel 3:1; Daniel 3:4; Daniel 4:30; Zechariah 5:11; 2 Chronicles 36:7; Jeremiah 27:16-22

echoes: Genesis 41; Genesis 39:21; Genesis 1:29; 2 Kings 24:1-17; 2 Chronicles 36:5-7; Jeremiah 25:1; Jeremiah 27:6; Isaiah 39:7; Esther 2; Judith 12:2; Tobit 1:10-11; 2 Maccabees 5:27; Daniel 10:2-3

settings.what: The story of the four young men at Nebuchadnezzar's court
settings.by: The narrator, who tells it in the third person (the book gives no name; the tradition names Daniel as the author of the whole)
settings.to: The Jewish exiles in Babylon in the sixth century (traditional view); Jews in Judea or the scattered communities under Seleucid rule in the second century BC (critical view)
settings.when: From the first siege of Jerusalem (605 BC on the traditional count) to the first year of Cyrus (539/538 BC)
settings.why: To show how a Jew can serve a foreign king and keep God's law, and to say that God, not Babylon's gods, gave Jerusalem and the vessels to Nebuchadnezzar (1:2). Knowing it was told to people who lived under foreign rulers changes it from a tale of one man into a rule for a community.
settings.readers: The Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt who read Daniel in the Greek translation; the writers of 1 Maccabees (2:59-60) who list the four's faith; Christians who read the chapter as a model of integrity in an unfriendly culture.
views: Traditional
The tale is Daniel's account (or that of his circle) of events in 605-538 BC, put to use for the exiles and then kept for later generations.
Critical

A collection of court tales (chapters 1-6) was gathered, perhaps in the third century BC, and given its final form in the crisis of 167-164 BC; the first hearers were Jews who lived among Gentile rulers and then were pressed to break the law.

settings.what: The head of the eunuchs answers Daniel's request
settings.by: Ashpenaz, the head of the eunuchs
settings.when: At the start of the three years of training, after Daniel asked not to be defiled (1:8)
settings.why: To show that the refusal is not about the official's own wishes: he fears for his head, since the king himself set the food. His answer explains why Daniel must find another way and why a ten-day test, which risks little, is the way he takes.
settings.readers: Jews who served in foreign courts and knew that a go-between could be punished for what a believer would not do.

settings.what: Daniel's proposal of a ten-day test
settings.to: The overseer (Hebrew melzar) whom the head of the eunuchs had put over the four young men
settings.when: In the first days of the three years of training, after the head of the eunuchs refused Daniel's request because he feared for his own life (1:10)
settings.why: To find a way for Daniel to avoid the king's food without making the official responsible. He offers a small, short and measurable test, and trusts the official's own eyes ("as you see"). Because Daniel asks and does not demand, the story shows how a faithful person can be cautious and still keep a limit.
settings.readers: Later Jews who ate at Gentile tables, as in Judith 12:2 and Tobit 1:10-11, and those in the Maccabean crisis who refused unclean food at risk of death (1 Maccabees 1:62-63).

title: The Statue and the Stone
sum: In the second year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that troubles him and will not let him sleep. He orders his magicians, enchanters, sorcerers and Chaldeans to tell him both the dream and its meaning, on pain of death. They answer, in Aramaic, that no one can do this, and the king orders all the wise men of Babylon killed, Daniel and his friends among them.

Daniel asks for time, and he and his three friends ask the God of the heavens for compassion. In a night vision the secret is shown, and Daniel answers with a hymn of praise. Before the king he says that no human wise man could tell the dream, but God has shown what will come: a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and iron mixed with clay, struck on its feet by a stone cut without hands, which becomes a mountain that fills the earth. The statue is a series of kingdoms; the stone, a kingdom God sets up that will not end. The king pays homage to Daniel and makes him ruler of Babylon.
readings: The four metals are four world empires in order; the stone is God's kingdom, which comes in the days of the last of them. The prophecy is a sixth-century word about the future, from Babylon to the end.
As a message to the persecuted

The four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece; the last is the divided kingdom of the Seleucids and Ptolemies, which the author's readers were suffering under. The message is that God will end it by his own act.
As a story of the wise man
The center is the contest of wisdom between the Chaldeans, who cannot, and Daniel, who can because God reveals. The statue is the occasion for a larger claim: God moves kings.

views.H: Traditional readers take the dream as given in 603 BC and fulfilled in Persia, Greece and Rome (or later); critical readers take the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece and the dream as shaped in the second century. The chapter fixes only the first kingdom (2:38). See the topic on the four kingdoms.
views.C: The Aramaic begins at 2:4, a pattern that carries to chapter 7. Critics see chapters 2 and 7 as a frame and the court tales as older; defenders see one author. The Persian loanwords, the schemes of metals (compare Hesiod) and the lack of any named Greek king are used on both sides.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition often reads the fourth kingdom as Edom, that is Rome, and the stone as the Messiah's kingdom (for the fourth kingdom, Leviticus Rabbah 13:5; Genesis Rabbah 2:4). Josephus did not explain the stone (Antiquities 10.210).
views.X: From Irenaeus and Hippolytus on, Christian writers took the stone as Christ and the kingdom as his; Jerome and Calvin have the same reading, with Rome as the fourth kingdom. Jesus' sayings on the stone (Matthew 21:44) are linked to this chapter.
views.F: Futurist readers (Walvoord and others) hold that the stone strikes the feet when the Roman empire is revived in a last form, and the kingdom that fills the earth is the future reign of Christ. Others hold it began with Christ and grows.

deep.b: The book changes language in the middle of verse 4 and stays in Aramaic until 7:28 (see the note at 2:4). The Plain keeps this visible in the section heading. The Aramaic words in the Hebrew Bible come from Aramaic, not Hebrew: malkuta "kingdom", 'elah "God", raz "secret".

deep.h: The four kingdoms across the book
deep.b: Chapter 2 gives the first image of the sequence; chapter 7 gives the second, as four beasts; chapter 8 names two of the kingdoms (8:20-21) and chapter 11 narrates the last. The identification of the four determines everything: if the fourth is Greece, the statue's feet are the Hellenistic kingdoms and the stone is God's rescue of the persecuted Jews; if the fourth is Rome, the stone is Christ's kingdom or a future one. The topic page The Four Kingdoms sets out the views once for the whole book.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a stone cut 'not by hands' and the altar of uncut stones
deep.b: God's law says an altar of stones must not be cut with a tool (Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:5-6; Joshua 8:31). Daniel's stone is "cut" but "not by hands", and it grows into a mountain, the place where God's house stands (Isaiah 2:2). My suggestion is that a first reader would have heard in the stone an altar-stone: a holy object God shapes himself, set against a statue that men made. That would make the end of the dream a temple and altar, the center of worship, replacing a world of man-made images. Commentators already link the stone to the temple mountain and to the Messiah; the added link to the uncut altar stones may overlap with published work. It is a suggestion from vocabulary and is not proved.
deep.refs: Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:5-6; Joshua 8:31; Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 2:34; Daniel 2:45

echoes: Genesis 41:1-45; Genesis 40:8; Isaiah 44:9-20; Isaiah 2:2; Jeremiah 27:5-7; Ezra 5:11; Daniel 4:34; Daniel 7:1-28; Daniel 8:20-21; Matthew 21:44; Revelation 1:1; Revelation 1:19

settings.what: The contest between the king and the Chaldeans
settings.by: Nebuchadnezzar and the court experts, as the story gives them
settings.to: Each other, in the king's court at Babylon, with the Jewish friends not yet present
settings.when: In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar (603/602 BC on the traditional count)
settings.why: To show that Babylon's learned men cannot do what the king asks, and by their own admission (2:11) say that only gods could. This clears the stage for a God who can. The scene also mocks a king whose word is law yet who asks the impossible, a picture that readers living under unpredictable rulers would know.
settings.readers: Exiles in Babylon, or later Jews who were taught that foreign wisdom had its limit.
views: Traditional
The exchange is a record of a real session at the Babylonian court, kept by Daniel.
Critical
A literary scene in the tale tradition; its Aramaic suggests it was told in the language of the diaspora and may have been written outside Judea.

settings.to: God, in his house, with his three friends present
settings.when: The night of the vision that showed the dream and its meaning, before he goes to the king
settings.why: To thank God before the king has heard anything: the praise comes first and the act follows. It names God's gifts (wisdom, power, knowledge of hidden things) and links them to his rule over kings. The hymn gives the book's theme in verse, and the four friends are "us" (2:23).
settings.readers: Jews who prayed these words in exile or in persecution; it is also a model for the thanksgivings of Qumran and the synagogue.

settings.what: Daniel's telling and interpretation of the dream
settings.by: Daniel, speaking as the interpreter (not as the one who knows)
settings.to: Nebuchadnezzar, in the presence of Arioch and the court
settings.when: Before the wise men of Babylon are put to death, the same day Daniel is brought in (2:24-26)
settings.why: To save the wise men, and above all to say that the God of the heavens governs kings and kingdoms and will end them all with a kingdom of his own. It tells the king his empire is given and limited; it promises the readers that their rulers' power is not final. The last words, that the dream is sure, give it the voice of prophecy.
settings.readers: Exiles in Babylon who needed to know that Babylon was not forever (traditional view); Jews in the second century BC under Antiochus IV, who read the last kingdom as the Greek empire and the stone as the end of Antiochus (critical view); later, Jewish and Christian readers who read it as pointing to the Messiah.
views: Traditional
A true prophecy given in 603 BC, covering Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, and the kingdom of God (Young, Baldwin and others).
Critical
A tale told as prophecy, the four kingdoms being Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, and the message about God's coming rescue of the persecuted in 167-164 BC (Collins and others).

settings.what: The king's homage and the promotion of Daniel and his friends
settings.to: Daniel and the court, in the king's presence
settings.when: Right after Daniel has told the dream and its meaning
settings.why: To show a king who has just heard that his empire is given and limited, and who answers by honoring the man and confessing his God (2:47). The gifts and the offerings are the king's way of paying a debt; the story does not say that Daniel took part in them. The scene also sets up the next chapter, where the three friends hold office in the province (2:49) and are accused for it.
settings.readers: Jews who held office under foreign rulers, as Joseph and Mordecai had, and who needed a story that showed a king rewarding a faithful man without asking him to give up his God.

title: The Golden Statue and the Furnace
sum: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden statue ninety feet tall on the plain of Dura, and calls every official of his empire to its dedication. At the sound of the music, everyone is to fall down and worship, or be thrown into a furnace. All the peoples obey. Certain Chaldeans tell the king that three Jews he has made administrators, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, do not worship the statue.

The king gives them one more chance. They answer that their God is able to rescue them, "and if he does not", they still will not serve his gods or worship the statue. He has the furnace heated seven times hotter, and the soldiers who carry them are killed by the flame. But the king sees four men walking loose in the fire, the fourth looking like a son of the gods. He calls the three out, unharmed, blesses their God for sending his angel, forbids any word against him, and promotes the three. The Greek Bible adds a prayer and a hymn inside the furnace.
readings: As a story of faithful refusal

Three men refuse to worship an image under threat of death, and God saves them. They give the pattern of civil disobedience for the sake of worship, and Jews and Christians afterward took them as martyr models.
As a story of the empire's power and its limit

The chapter sets state power (the order, the music, the furnace) against a God who is bigger. The king's rage is repeated in a list of officials and instruments in a way that makes the empire's pomp look both grand and absurd.
As a parable for the persecuted
For Jews under Antiochus IV, who forced them to give up the law, the tale says that those who stand firm may be rescued, and if they are not, their witness still stands.

views.H: On the traditional dating this is an event in Nebuchadnezzar's reign, perhaps about 587-586 BC if the Greek date holds. On the Maccabean dating it is a story set in Babylon and written for those under Antiochus IV, whose forced worship (1 Maccabees 1:41-50) it recalls.
views.C: Critics stress the Greek-sounding instruments (3:5), the Persian officials' titles and the repeated lists, and read the chapter as a tale shaped for retelling; defenders give the same words a sixth-century place (see the notes at 3:2 and 3:5). No outside source mentions the statue or the furnace.
views.J: Jewish tradition treats the three as martyrs who sanctified God's name (Pesachim 53b). In Pesachim 118a the angel in charge of hail offers to cool the furnace and Gabriel objects and offers to cool it from within. Their refusal is a model for kiddush hashem.
views.X: Christian readers see the three as models of faithful witness (1 Clement 45:6-7; Hebrews 11:34) and the fourth figure as an angel or as the Son of God before his birth; the church uses the Song of the Three at morning prayer.
views.F: Some futurist readers compare the statue to the image of the beast in Revelation 13:14-15, which also demands worship on pain of death; others call this a type of the last test. Revelation does not quote the chapter directly.

deep.b: The three give two answers in one speech. First they say God can save them and will (3:17); then "and if he does not", they will not bow (3:18). The first is faith in power, the second is faith without a guarantee. The story's rescue shows God can, but the answer to the second, whether God also will not leave his servants to die, is left to other stories. In 1 Maccabees 2:59-60 the three are named with Daniel among those saved by faith; in 4 Maccabees (16:21) they stand beside the martyrs who died. Both uses are in the tradition.

The king sees a fourth whose appearance is "like that of a son of the gods" (3:25) and calls him "his angel" (3:28). The note at 3:25 gives the options. The text does not say whether the figure is the angel who shut the lions' mouths (6:22) or another being, and it records no word from him.

deep.h: The Greek additions: the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three
deep.b: In the Greek Daniel, between 3:23 and 3:24, comes a long prayer and hymn. They are not in the Hebrew and Aramaic text and so not in the Plain, but they are Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and they have been used in worship far more than any other part of Daniel 3. The variant at 3:23 summarizes them; the note at 3:24 describes their use in the liturgy. The question of whether they belong to Daniel is the subject of the book-wide "Where Christians differ" card.

echoes: Genesis 11:1-9; Exodus 5:2; Isaiah 43:2; Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 29:22; 2 Kings 18:33-35; Daniel 6:1-28; 1 Maccabees 1:41-64; 1 Maccabees 2:59-60; 4 Maccabees 16:21; Hebrews 11:34; Revelation 13:14-15

settings.what: The herald's order to worship the statue
settings.by: A herald speaking for King Nebuchadnezzar
settings.to: The gathered officials of the empire and the peoples, nations and languages standing before the statue on the plain of Dura
settings.when: At the statue's dedication, on a day the Greek version places in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year
settings.why: To bind every official in public loyalty with one act and one signal, backed by the furnace. A king who rules many peoples and gods asks for a shared sign of obedience. Knowing the crowd is the whole empire makes the three friends' refusal not a private matter: they refuse in public, in front of the world.
settings.readers: Exiles who might be asked to take part in state worship; Jews under Antiochus IV, whose edict forced all his kingdom to one worship (1 Maccabees 1:41-43); later, Christians asked to burn incense to the emperor (the topic on ruler worship).
views: Traditional
A real event in Babylon. No Babylonian text mentions the statue, which is not surprising for a story told from the Jews' side.
Critical
A tale built on the type of the tyrant's decree; its details (instruments, officials) are for the storyteller's effect.

settings.by: Certain Chaldean men, the king's learned class
settings.when: Right after the music has sounded and the peoples have bowed
settings.why: To bring the Jews down. They use the king's own order against three men whose promotion (2:49) they resent, and they put it as a charge of disloyalty to the king himself: "they have not given you a thought". The accusation shows that the pressure was political and personal as well as religious, as in Esther 3:8 and Daniel 6.
settings.readers: Jews of later centuries who lived under rulers' officials and could be denounced to them by neighbors, as in Esther 3:8 and Daniel 6.

settings.what: The king's challenge to the three
settings.to: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, brought before him
settings.when: After the accusation, before the furnace
settings.why: To give the three a second chance to bow when the music sounds, and then to turn the matter into a contest between himself and their God: "Which god is there that can save you from my hands?" (3:15). Like Pharaoh's and the Assyrian commander's boasts, it asks the readers whether any god can save them from a king.
settings.readers: Jews who were asked to take part in state worship under threat of death, and who heard in the king's boast the same boast that earlier kings had made and lost (note at 3:15).

settings.what: The three friends' answer to the king
settings.to: Nebuchadnezzar, in his rage, before the furnace
settings.when: After the king offers them one more chance to bow when the music sounds
settings.why: To say they will not discuss it, because their decision does not depend on whether they are rescued. They put God's power and their own loyalty side by side without making God owe them anything. For readers who might be asked to give up the law on pain of death, this is the model answer, and for those who died anyway it is a defense of their choice.
settings.readers: Jews in the Maccabean crisis (1 Maccabees 2:59-60); later Jewish and Christian martyrs (1 Clement 45:6-7).
views: Rescue not promised
'If he does not' admits that God may let them die, and their refusal still holds.
Rescue expected
Some read the sentence as 'He will save us; and if (he does) not, we will still not bow', that is, as certainty about God's help.

settings.to: His court, then any people, nation or language of his kingdom
settings.when: After the three come out of the furnace
settings.why: To protect the three and their God by law, as 2:47 praised him by words. The king blesses the God of the three and threatens any who speak against him. It is a royal statement, not a conversion: Babylon will tolerate one more god. Compare the decrees of Darius (6:25-27) and, outside the book, Cyrus (Ezra 1:2-4).
settings.readers: Jews who lived under rulers who allowed their worship, or who forbade it; the Greek-reading communities, who had the prayer and the song as well.

settings.what: The king sees the fourth figure and calls the three out
settings.to: His counselors, then the three, with the officials gathered round
settings.when: Right after the three are thrown in
settings.why: To show the king, who had ordered the fire, seeing what he cannot explain and then speaking to the three as "servants of the Most High God" (3:26). The officials who crowd round see that the fire had no power over their bodies. The scene turns the king's challenge in 3:15 into a confession.
settings.readers: Jews under pressure from rulers and their officials, who needed to hear that the empire's own witnesses saw the rescue.
